about.title: Fireflies Fall Into Step
about.math: Kuramoto model: each phase θᵢ turns at its own speed ωᵢ plus K·r·sin(ψ − θᵢ), where r e^{iψ} is the average of all of them. K grows over the video.
about.aha: Below a critical pull nothing happens; just above it, order appears suddenly, a phase transition. No firefly is in charge.
about.why: Heart pacemaker cells, applause, power grids, pendulum clocks on one beam and the Millennium Bridge wobble.

about.title: The Endless Rise (Shepard Scale)
about.math: Each step plays C, C#, D … in six octaves at once, loudest in the middle (a bell over pitch). After 12 steps the chord is exactly the same as at the start.
about.aha: The highest note fades out as a new lowest note fades in, so the ear never hears the climb end. The video lasts exactly 6 × 12 steps, so it loops seamlessly.
about.why: Used in film scores for endless tension (Dunkirk) and in Super Mario 64’s endless staircase.

about.title: Three Suns: The Figure Eight
about.math: Three equal masses pulled by Newton’s gravity, starting from Chenciner and Montgomery’s initial conditions (x₁ = −x₂ ≈ (0.970, −0.243), x₃ = 0). Period ≈ 6.326.
about.aha: The general three-body problem has no formula and is usually chaotic, yet this one dance repeats exactly. The ghost started 0.003 away and slowly leaves the dance.
about.why: Found numerically by Cris Moore in 1993, proved to exist in 2000.

about.title: The Fastest Slide
about.math: Frictionless beads slide from the same start to the same end along a straight line, an arc, a parabola and a cycloid (x = R(φ − sin φ), y = −R(1 − cos φ)).
about.aha: The straight line is shortest but slowest; the cycloid dives steeply, gains speed early and wins.
about.why: Johann Bernoulli’s 1696 challenge, solved by Newton overnight.

about.title: Tautochrone: All Arrive Together
about.math: On a cycloid the distance s along the curve from the bottom obeys s″ = −(g/4R)·s, so every bead reaches the bottom after π√(R/g), wherever it starts.
about.aha: Higher beads have farther to go but the slope is steeper: it balances exactly. Huygens used this to build a more accurate pendulum clock.
